``` r
#> ecxwb2        -1667.78 0.03
#> ecxwb1p3      -1659.75 0.00
#> ecxwb2p3      -1660.24 0.00

#> ecxll4        -1662.58 0.01
#> ecxll3        -1651.78 0.00
#> ecxhormebc4   -1676.32 0.63
#> 
#> 
#> Summary of weighted N(S)EC posterior estimates:
#> NB: Model set contains a combination of ECx and NEC
#>     models, and is therefore a model averaged
#>     combination of NEC and NSEC estimates.
#>        Estimate  Q2.5 Q97.5
#> N(S)EC    -1.52 -2.09  0.72
#> 
#> 
#> Bayesian R2 estimates:
#>               Estimate Est.Error Q2.5 Q97.5
#> nec4param         0.98      0.00 0.98  0.98
#> nechorme          0.98      0.00 0.98  0.99
#> nechormepwr01     0.98      0.00 0.98  0.99
#> ecx4param         0.98      0.00 0.98  0.98
#> ecxwb1            0.98      0.00 0.98  0.98
#> ecxwb2            0.98      0.00 0.98  0.98
#> ecxwb1p3          0.98      0.00 0.98  0.98
#> ecxwb2p3          0.98      0.00 0.98  0.98
#> ecxll5            0.98      0.00 0.98  0.98
#> ecxll4            0.98      0.00 0.98  0.98
#> ecxll3            0.98      0.00 0.98  0.98
#> ecxhormebc4       0.98      0.00 0.98  0.99
```

As in the sections above, the N(S)EC in that summary is on the scale the model
was fitted on, `log(diuron_adj)`. `nsec()` and `ecx()` with `xform = exp` return
the NSEC and the effect concentrations in µg/L. The summary reads the NEC
equations by their `nec` parameter, and `nsec()` reads every equation by its
NSEC, so the two averages differ slightly.


``` r
# Bound once: the figure below draws its reference lines from the same NSEC.
pam_ne <- nsec(fit_pam, xform = exp)
rbind(
  data.frame(estimate = "NSEC", t(pam_ne)),
  data.frame(estimate = "EC10", t(ecx(fit_pam, ecx_val = 10, xform = exp))),
  data.frame(estimate = "EC50", t(ecx(fit_pam, ecx_val = 50, xform = exp)))
)
#>   estimate       Q50      Q2.5    Q97.5
#> 1     NSEC 0.2166200 0.1197926 2.085665
#> 2     EC10 0.4768297 0.4020541 2.140971
#> 3     EC50 1.9990215 1.8025923 2.733051
```

The three estimates are ordered as they should be --- 0.217, 0.477 and 1.999
µg/L --- and their upper bounds are not. The NSEC reaches 2.086 and the EC10
2.141, both above the EC50 median, while the EC50 interval is the narrowest of
the three at 1.803 to 2.733.

A model-averaged estimate is a mixture, and the median and the tail of a mixture
can be set by different components. Three equations hold 0.89 of the weight here
and all place the threshold low: `ecxhormebc4` (0.632) at 0.225 (0.120--0.292),
`ecxwb1` (0.152) at 0.178 (0.114--0.231) and `ecxll5` (0.104) at 0.182
(0.116--0.235). None has an upper bound above 0.3, and the averaged median of
0.217 is theirs. The averaged upper bound is not. `nec4param` places a threshold
at 2.106 (1.812--2.357) on a weight of 0.04. That is more than the 0.025 of the
mixture above its 97.5th percentile, and the percentile, 2.086, falls inside the
interval of `nec4param`. `ecxwb2` places its threshold at 1.606 (1.127--1.923)
on 0.03, wholly below that percentile. The tail is set by `nec4param` alone.

Each equation's own threshold, against the weight it holds, is below. The
estimator follows the equation: `nec()` where the equation has a `nec`
parameter, `nsec()` where it does not.


``` r
pam_wi <- summary(fit_pam)$mod_weights[, "wi"]
pam_thr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pam_wi), function(m) {
  one <- pull_out(fit_pam, model = m)
  v <- if (m %in% models()$nec) nec(one, xform = exp) else nsec(one, xform = exp)
  data.frame(equation = m, wi = pam_wi[[m]], est = v[[1]], lo = v[[2]], hi = v[[3]])
}))
pam_thr$equation <- reorder(factor(pam_thr$equation), pam_thr$est)
pam_thr[order(-pam_thr$wi), ]
#>         equation          wi       est        lo        hi
#> 12   ecxhormebc4 0.632296110 0.2253004 0.1198070 0.2919767
#> 5         ecxwb1 0.152248197 0.1783674 0.1138664 0.2312553
#> 9         ecxll5 0.104445750 0.1818665 0.1163803 0.2354512
#> 1      nec4param 0.040203961 2.1061274 1.8122728 2.3572905
#> 6         ecxwb2 0.031898516 1.6064799 1.1271047 1.9231924
#> 4      ecx4param 0.010788705 0.7233387 0.4295838 0.9726407
#> 2       nechorme 0.007327807 0.6405761 0.5637219 0.7082179
#> 10        ecxll4 0.006234811 0.7123232 0.3848781 0.9396482
#> 3  nechormepwr01 0.005823848 0.6407759 0.5636155 0.7085278
#> 8       ecxwb2p3 0.004323472 0.7724442 0.5643879 0.9579842
#> 7       ecxwb1p3 0.002258370 0.1997385 0.1152668 0.2814606
#> 11        ecxll3 0.002150454 0.4185043 0.1879688 0.5619532

ggplot(pam_thr, aes(x = est, y = equation)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = pam_ne[[2]], xmax = pam_ne[[3]],
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#2c6a5a", alpha = 0.07) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = pam_ne[[1]], colour = "#2c6a5a") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = pam_ne[[3]], colour = "#2c6a5a", linetype = 2) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, colour = wi)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = wi, size = wi)) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "grey80", high = "#2c6a5a",
                        name = "model\nweight") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 5, guide = "none") +
  log_x +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "Threshold (µg/L)", y = NULL)
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-fig-pam-thresholds-1.png" alt="plot of chunk fig-pam-thresholds" width="85%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk fig-pam-thresholds</p>
</div>

The solid line is the model-averaged median and the dashed line its upper
bound, with the averaged interval shaded. The ordering is what the paragraph
above states in numbers: the three darkest points sit at the left of the range,
the two furthest to the right sit an order of magnitude away from them and are
pale, with `nec4param` on the dashed line itself, and between them the weight
is unrelated to the position. An
equation's threshold and the weight it holds are separate quantities, and that
is what lets 0.04 of the weight decide where the averaged interval ends.

The same draws are visible in the figure below. The credible band steps down at
about 2 µg/L, its upper edge falling from about 0.58 to about 0.30, because the
equations that place a threshold there hold the curve near the control until it
and drop afterwards. Less than a tenth of the weight has no effect on the median
and still decides where the interval ends, which is a reason to read a
model-averaged interval against the weights rather than on its own.


``` r
autoplot(fit_pam, group = "climate", group_aes = "colour") + log_x
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-fig-pam-1.png" alt="plot of chunk fig-pam" width="60%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk fig-pam</p>
</div>

`climate` is not in the fitted formula --- the model estimates a deviation per
chamber, not per scenario --- so `autoplot()` takes it from the columns `bnec()`
retained from the supplied data and labels the legend "climate (not fitted)".
The curve and the band are pooled over the three scenarios, and the colour marks
the observations only.

The scenarios overlap over most of the series. The scenario means of `yield`
differ by at most 0.014 at 0.1, 0.29, 0.96 and 2.9 µg/L, and separate only at
9.6 and 29 µg/L, where they are 0.052, 0.040, 0.022 and 0.027, 0.006, 0.000 ---
a separation between quantities that have already fallen to a twelfth of the
control. @flores2021 report the same result from these data, giving a
probability of 0.615 and 0.539 that yield differs between the warming scenarios.

The colour endpoint has five concentrations and 45 chambers of four fragments.
Fitting equations of three and of four curve parameters to it separately shows
where the design runs out:


``` r
three_par <- bnec(proportion ~ crf(log(diuron_adj), c("ecxll3", "ecxwb1p3")) + ogl(chamber),
                  data = coral_colour, family = Beta(link = "identity"),
                  seed = 228, refresh = 0)

four_par <- bnec(proportion ~ crf(log(diuron_adj), c("nec4param", "ecx4param")) + ogl(chamber),
                 data = coral_colour, family = Beta(link = "identity"),
                 seed = 228, refresh = 0)
```


``` r
sampled_badly <- function(fit, label) {
  worst <- vapply(rhat(fit), function(x) max(x$rhat_vals), numeric(1))
  divergent <- vapply(names(worst), function(m) {
    np <- brms::nuts_params(pull_out(fit, model = m)$fit)
    sum(np$Value[np$Parameter == "divergent__"])
  }, numeric(1))
  data.frame(curve = label, equation = names(worst),
             divergent = divergent, max_rhat = round(worst, 4),
             row.names = NULL)
}
rbind(sampled_badly(three_par, "three parameters"),
      sampled_badly(four_par, "four parameters"))
#>              curve  equation divergent max_rhat
#> 1 three parameters    ecxll3         6   1.0042
#> 2 three parameters  ecxwb1p3         0   1.0024
#> 3  four parameters nec4param      4334   1.0995
#> 4  four parameters ecx4param      1024   1.0092
```

Neither three-parameter equation fails the screen: `ecxll3` records 6 divergent
transitions and `ecxwb1p3` none, and both have an R-hat of 1.004 or below.
`nec4param` records 4334 divergent transitions in its 8000 retained draws and
`ecx4param` 1024, at R-hats of 1.099 and 1.009. More than half of the
transitions of `nec4param` diverged, and an eighth of those of `ecx4param`.

A divergent transition is recorded where the sampler's step size is too large
for the curvature of the posterior at that point, so the simulated path departs
from the one the equations describe. A parameter the data do not constrain
produces exactly that curvature, in a posterior nearly flat along one direction
and sharp across it. R-hat asks a different question --- whether the chains of
one fit arrived at the same distribution --- and here it fails for `nec4param`
and passes for `ecx4param`.

R-hat alone would therefore pass `ecx4param`. At `bnec()`'s default run length
its R-hat is 1.009, inside the cutoff of 1.01 and within 0.007 of the two
three-parameter equations, while an eighth of its transitions diverged. Of the
two diagnostics in the table, only the divergent transitions report the problem.
On the single zinc plate they were also the only one of the three that
`check_sampling()` reports to fail `ecxexp`. A check read alone can pass an
equation that another check fails.


``` r
autoplot(three_par, group = "climate", group_aes = "colour") + log_x
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-fig-three-par-1.png" alt="plot of chunk fig-three-par" width="60%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk fig-three-par</p>
</div>


``` r
autoplot(four_par, group = "climate", group_aes = "colour") + log_x
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-fig-four-par-1.png" alt="plot of chunk fig-four-par" width="60%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk fig-four-par</p>
</div>

The figures show where those divergences come from. Nothing between 2.9 and 29
µg/L tells a four-parameter equation where its lower asymptote sits, because the
colour design has no observation across that tenfold range. At 10 µg/L the
four-parameter credible band is 0.65 wide on a response that runs from 0 to
about 0.9, so it covers most of the values the endpoint can take; the
three-parameter band is 0.31 there. Both close to about 0.06 at the top of the
series, where the observations resume. A three-parameter equation fixes the
lower asymptote instead of estimating it, and so has nothing to place in the
gap.

The four-parameter equations are worse served than the gap alone suggests. What
they have to estimate a lower asymptote from is one concentration, and the
reading at that concentration is of fragments that had bleached completely.

The climate scenarios separate in these two figures where they did not in
`fit_pam`. The scenario means of `proportion` are 0.779, 0.737 and 0.672 at
0.96 µg/L and 0.728, 0.611 and 0.456 at 2.9, a spread of 0.27 on a response
running to about 0.9, and the 2100 points sit below the 2018 points at every
concentration above the control. @flores2021 report a probability of 0.956 and
0.970 that the colour index differs between the warming scenarios, against
0.615 and 0.539 for yield. Neither figure fits that difference: both curves are
pooled over the scenarios, and separating them would need `climate` in the
formula or a `bnec_group()` call over it.

The threshold estimates differ in the same way. The three-parameter set returns
an NSEC of 1.61 µg/L (0.63--4.53), as its figure reports. The four-parameter set
returns an N(S)EC of 4.55 (1.74--24.80): a median inside the unsampled interval
between 2.9 and 29 µg/L, and an upper bound of the same order as the highest
concentration tested, which is 29. Both sets were fitted to the same 180
observations.

#301 proposes restricting a model set by the number of curve parameters for
this reason.

The colour score has exactly one observation on the `Beta` boundary, which
follows from the rescaling described above, and the yield endpoint has 63
readings at zero.
Neither is a defect in the data; both are decisions about the response that have
to be made before the family is chosen, and `vignette("example6")` covers them.

# Case study 3

<small>*Phytotoxicity of photosystem II herbicides to coral*</small>

`herbicide` [@jones2003] holds the effective quantum yield of photosystem II in
the symbiotic dinoflagellates of the coral *Seriatopora hystrix*, measured after
a ten-hour exposure to each of seven photosystem II inhibiting herbicides. Three
replicate containers of four corals were held at each concentration. The report
is at <https://doi.org/10.3354/meps261149>.

The endpoint is the same quantity as `coral_pam`'s `yield`, and the two studies
are connected by more than that. @jones2003 found the effect of diuron to be
inversely related to temperature, which is the observation @flores2021 tested
two decades later by crossing diuron with warming.


``` r
data(herbicide)
ggplot(herbicide, aes(x = concentration, y = fvfm, colour = herbicide)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~herbicide, ncol = 2, scales = "free_x") +
  log_x +
  scale_colour_hue(guide = "none") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(1.2, "lines")) +
  labs(x = "Concentration (ug/L)", y = "Effective quantum yield")
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-fig-herbicide-raw-1.png" alt="plot of chunk fig-herbicide-raw" width="72%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk fig-herbicide-raw</p>
</div>

Effective quantum yield declines with concentration in all seven, and the
concentration at which it does so differs by two orders of magnitude between
them. Yield is at half its lowest-dose mean by 1 µg/L of irgarol and 3 µg/L of
diuron or ametryn, against 100 µg/L of tebuthiuron and 300 of simazine, which is
the highest concentration simazine was tested at.

Seven herbicides are a fixed set chosen for their interest, not a sample from a
population of herbicides, so shrinking them towards a common curve answers a
different question from the one being asked, and their functional forms may
differ. `bnec_group()` fits each level separately and returns one object. This
call uses `decline` rather than `"all"`, which is what Figure 11 of @fisher2024
was fitted with.


``` r
fits_herb <- bnec_group(fvfm ~ crf(log(concentration), "decline"),
                        data = herbicide, group_var = "herbicide",
                        family = Beta(link = "identity"),
                        seed = 228, refresh = 0)
```

Each herbicide is screened separately because each was fitted separately. A
failed equation is removed from that herbicide without discarding successful
fits of the same equation for the other six.


``` r
fits_herb <- screen_models(fits_herb, group_action = "per_level")
#> Screening level "ametryn".
#> All 11 candidate models passed the sampler screen (Rhat <= 1.01, ESS >= 400, divergences <= 10).
#> Screening level "atrazine".
#> All 11 candidate models passed the sampler screen (Rhat <= 1.01, ESS >= 400, divergences <= 10).
#> Screening level "diuron".
#> All 11 candidate models passed the sampler screen (Rhat <= 1.01, ESS >= 400, divergences <= 10).
#> Screening level "hexazinone".
#> All 11 candidate models passed the sampler screen (Rhat <= 1.01, ESS >= 400, divergences <= 10).
#> Screening level "irgarol".
#> All 11 candidate models passed the sampler screen (Rhat <= 1.01, ESS >= 400, divergences <= 10).
#> Screening level "simazine".
#> All 11 candidate models passed the sampler screen (Rhat <= 1.01, ESS >= 400, divergences <= 10).
#> Screening level "tebuthiuron".
#> All 11 candidate models passed the sampler screen (Rhat <= 1.01, ESS >= 400, divergences <= 10).
```

Every equation passes for every herbicide, so each herbicide's model average is
taken over all eleven equations of `decline`.

`summary()` on a `bayesnecgroupfit` prints a full summary for every level, which
for seven herbicides is several hundred lines. What the sections below draw on
is the model weights, and those are worth seeing together:


``` r
herb_wi <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(f, lev) {
  w <- summary(f)$mod_weights[, "wi"]
  data.frame(herbicide = lev, equation = names(w), wi = as.numeric(w))
}, fits_herb$fits, fits_herb$levels))
# Ordered by the weight each equation takes over all seven, so that the
# equations the set actually uses sit together at the top.
herb_wi$equation <- reorder(factor(herb_wi$equation), herb_wi$wi, sum)

ggplot(herb_wi, aes(x = herbicide, y = equation, fill = wi)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(wi >= 0.05, sprintf("%.2f", wi), "")),
            size = 2.7, colour = "grey15") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#2c6a5a", name = "weight",
                      limits = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
        axis.line = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-fig-herb-weights-1.png" alt="plot of chunk fig-herb-weights" width="85%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk fig-herb-weights</p>
</div>

The seven do not agree on which equation describes them. Tebuthiuron puts half
its weight on `ecxwb2p3`, which takes no more than 0.08 anywhere else, and
hexazinone puts 0.62 on `ecxll3`, which four of the others give less than 0.05.
Counting the labelled cells, those of 0.05 or more, ametryn and irgarol spread
their weight over four equations, diuron over five and simazine over six, and no
equation holds more than 0.29 at any of the four. That
is the case for fitting the levels separately rather than shrinking them towards
a common curve: the curve they would be shrunk towards is not one the data agree
on.

Toxicity estimates for the seven herbicides span two orders of magnitude.
`nec()` returns each herbicide's N(S)EC, back-transformed from the fitted scale:


``` r
nec(fits_herb, xform = exp)
#>         level        Q50      Q2.5      Q97.5 bound_Q50 bound_Q2.5 bound_Q97.5
#> 1     ametryn  0.1977117 0.1200018  0.6190542                                 
#> 2    atrazine  1.1204227 0.3391386  2.4749705                                 
#> 3      diuron  0.1518601 0.1101068  0.1952373                                 
#> 4  hexazinone  0.6309808 0.2358972  1.6390054                                 
#> 5     irgarol  0.1352690 0.1065716  0.1744017                                 
#> 6    simazine  4.3910362 1.1747670 11.4193765                                 
#> 7 tebuthiuron 10.5215413 4.2807827 14.0294702
```

It runs from irgarol at 0.135 µg/L (0.107--0.174) and diuron at 0.152
(0.110--0.195), through ametryn at 0.198, hexazinone at 0.631 and atrazine at
1.120, to simazine at 4.391 and tebuthiuron at 10.522 (4.281--14.029).

The N(S)EC is a threshold, the concentration at which the response first departs
from the control, and it is not what @jones2003 report. They report EC50s, the
concentration at which yield is halved, so the comparison with the source study
is against `ecx()`:


``` r
ecx(fits_herb, ecx_val = 50, xform = exp)
#>         level         Q50        Q2.5       Q97.5 bound_Q50 bound_Q2.5 bound_Q97.5
#> 1     ametryn   1.4979215   1.4119204   1.6003311                                 
#> 2    atrazine  39.4891915  34.9655932  44.3233018                                 
#> 3      diuron   2.0375062   1.9023437   2.1945167                                 
#> 4  hexazinone   7.4290120   6.7643451   8.1054997                                 
#> 5     irgarol   0.5397205   0.4909131   0.5984148                                 
#> 6    simazine 123.6660452 112.2513566 135.7756253                                 
#> 7 tebuthiuron  90.4028480  84.0568413  95.4276526
```

Their values are irgarol 0.7 µg/L, ametryn 1.7, diuron 2.3, hexazinone 8.8,
atrazine 45, simazine 150 and tebuthiuron 175. Six of the seven agree closely,
the published figure sitting between 13 and 30 per cent above the one here, and
the ordering of those six is the same in both. Tebuthiuron is the exception at
roughly half the published value, and it is also the herbicide whose ordering
differs: here it is more toxic than simazine, and in the source study less so.

The two are not derived the same way. @jones2003 interpolate linearly between
the tested concentrations, in ToxCalc 5.0, while the values above come from a
model average over eleven fitted curves. Linear interpolation across a
log-spaced series cuts the chord of a curve that is concave over that interval,
which places the half-effect concentration higher than a fitted curve does, and
the published value is higher in all seven. That six of the seven agree within a
third is the agreement worth having. Nothing in these data settles which
estimate is closer to the truth for tebuthiuron.


``` r
ggplot(group_curves(fits_herb), aes(x = x_e, colour = level, fill = level)) +
  geom_polygon(aes(y = y_ci), colour = NA, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_e), linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = x_r, y = y_r), alpha = 0.6, size = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = nec_vals), colour = "grey50") +
  facet_wrap(~level, ncol = 2, scales = "free_x") +
  log_x +
  scale_colour_hue(guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_hue(guide = "none") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(1.2, "lines")) +
  labs(x = "Concentration (ug/L)", y = "Effective quantum yield")
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-fig-herbicides-1.png" alt="plot of chunk fig-herbicides" width="72%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk fig-herbicides</p>
</div>

Yield declines with concentration in all seven, and the fitted band follows the
observations down in each, with the N(S)EC rule at or a little before the
concentration where the points leave the control level. The response axis is shared and the concentration axis
is not, so the panels are comparable in level and not in position: the seven
curves have much the same shape and sit at different concentrations. Fitting
each level separately is what allows the shape to differ between them. Here it
largely does not, and what separates the herbicides is where the curve falls
rather than how.


``` r
cmp_herb <- compare_posterior(fits_herb, comparison = "n(s)ec")
cmp_herb$prob_diff
#>                comparison        prob  prob_lower  prob_upper censored_first censored_second
#> 1        ametryn-atrazine 0.017752219 0.017752219 0.017752219              0               0
#> 2          ametryn-diuron 0.848981123 0.848981123 0.848981123              0               0
#> 3      ametryn-hexazinone 0.039754969 0.039754969 0.039754969              0               0

#> 9        atrazine-irgarol 0.989498687 0.989498687 0.989498687              0               0
#> 10      atrazine-simazine 0.034879360 0.034879360 0.034879360              0               0
#> 11   atrazine-tebuthiuron 0.008876110 0.008876110 0.008876110              0               0
#> 12      diuron-hexazinone 0.012501563 0.012501563 0.012501563              0               0
#> 13         diuron-irgarol 0.726715839 0.726715839 0.726715839              0               0
#> 14        diuron-simazine 0.011001375 0.011001375 0.011001375              0               0
#> 15     diuron-tebuthiuron 0.008251031 0.008251031 0.008251031              0               0
#> 16     hexazinone-irgarol 0.988873609 0.988873609 0.988873609              0               0
#> 17    hexazinone-simazine 0.018002250 0.018002250 0.018002250              0               0
#> 18 hexazinone-tebuthiuron 0.008376047 0.008376047 0.008376047              0               0
#> 19       irgarol-simazine 0.010751344 0.010751344 0.010751344              0               0
#> 20    irgarol-tebuthiuron 0.008376047 0.008376047 0.008376047              0               0
#> 21   simazine-tebuthiuron 0.086510814 0.086510814 0.086510814              0               0
```

`prob_diff` gives the probability that the first level of each pair has the
higher estimate, so a value near 0 or 1 separates two herbicides and one near
0.5 does not. Of the 21 pairs the clearest are those of tebuthiuron against the
five most potent herbicides, from 0.0083 for ametryn and diuron to 0.0089 for
atrazine. The least separated is diuron against irgarol at 0.727, the two most
potent of the set, whose intervals overlap over most of their length; the next
are atrazine against hexazinone at 0.837 and ametryn against diuron at 0.849.

The 21 pairwise probabilities reduce seven posteriors to one number each, and
those posteriors are in `posterior_data`:


``` r
# Figure 11 of Fisher et al. (2024) is this display for these seven herbicides,
# and this reproduces it. The posteriors are on the fitted scale, log(ug/L), and
# exp() returns them to concentration so that the axis reads in the units the
# estimates are reported in, as every other figure here does.
herb_post <- cmp_herb$posterior_data
herb_post$value <- exp(herb_post$value)

ggplot(data = herb_post, mapping = aes(x = value)) +
  geom_density(mapping = aes(group = model, colour = model, fill = model),
               alpha = 0.3) +
  log_x +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "Concentration (ug/L)", y = "Density",
       fill = "Model", colour = "Model")
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-fig-cmp-herbicides-1.png" alt="plot of chunk fig-cmp-herbicides" width="95%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk fig-cmp-herbicides</p>
</div>

This reproduces Figure 11 of @fisher2024. Two things the pairwise probabilities
do not say are visible in the densities.

The two most potent overlap almost entirely. Irgarol at 0.135 and diuron at
0.152 have intervals of 0.107 to 0.174 and 0.110 to 0.195, so one sits almost
inside the other; that is what a `prob_diff` of 0.727 looks like as a
distribution. Ametryn overlaps both only in part: its median, 0.198, lies above
both of their upper bounds, and its interval runs on to 0.619.

The posteriors differ in width as much as in position. From end to end,
irgarol's interval spans a factor of 1.6 and diuron's 1.8, against 9.7 for
simazine and 7.3 for atrazine. Hexazinone and simazine are a factor of seven
apart in median and still overlap, because both are poorly determined:
hexazinone's interval spans a factor of 6.9.

Several are bimodal. Tebuthiuron has a second mode near 7 µg/L, simazine one
near 10 and hexazinone one near 1.6, which is the model-averaging mixture traced
in `fit_pam`: a low-weight equation placing its threshold elsewhere, visible in
the tail of the average and not in its median.

The pairing matters for what this comparison may be used on. `compare_posterior()`
pairs the draws of two posteriors by a random permutation, which approximates the
difference of two independent posteriors and is valid only where the posteriors
come from separate fits. `bnec_group()` fits every level separately, so that
holds here.

The two `bnec_group()` fits are screened per level, as specified in their calls.
Their independently fitted levels can retain different equation sets when an
equation samples adequately for one level and fails for another. Two levels of
a single fit share draws, and permuting them discards
the correlation between them, widening the difference and pulling `prob_diff`
towards 0.5 --- so a contrast between parts of one fit needs draw-wise
differencing and must not be routed through this function.

## Contrasts from a joint refit

That restriction is what a joint refit removes. `bnec_joint()` takes the
per-level fits and builds one model that includes every level at once, each level
keeping the equation its own weights favour and its own copy of that equation's
parameters. A difference between two levels is then a difference between
coefficients of one fit, taken draw by draw, and it needs no permutation.

No equation is named here. Each level's is read from the weights the
`bnec_group()` fit already computed, so the refit is of what each herbicide
separately favoured rather than of one form imposed on all seven. The call comes
after `screen_models()` above, so it refits the screened set --- the equations
each herbicide retained --- and not the set as first fitted.


``` r
herb_joint <- bnec_joint(fits_herb, seed = 228, refresh = 0)
```


``` r
herb_joint
#> Object of class bayesnecjointfit
#> 
#>   equations         : ametryn = ecxll4, atrazine = ecxwb1, diuron = ecx4param, hexazinone = ecxll3, irgarol = ecx4param, simazine = ecxll3, tebuthiuron = ecxwb2p3 
#>   grouping variable : herbicide 
#>   levels            : ametryn, atrazine, diuron, hexazinone, irgarol, simazine, tebuthiuron 
#>   family            : beta (link = identity) 
#>   dispersion        : per level 
#>   weight at level   : ametryn 0.293, atrazine 0.383, diuron 0.279, hexazinone 0.623, irgarol 0.291, simazine 0.292, tebuthiuron 0.504 
#> 
#> Each level has its own equation and its own curve parameters in
#> one posterior; read them from the draws as
#> b_<parameter><level tag>_Intercept, the tags being ametryn = ametrynLv1, atrazine = atrazineLv2, diuron = diuronLv3, hexazinone = hexazinoneLv4, irgarol = irgarolLv5, simazine = simazineLv6, tebuthiuron = tebuthiuronLv7.
#> ecx(), nsec() and nec() return one row per level, and autoplot()
#> draws one panel per level.
```

Five different equations are composed across the seven herbicides: `ecxll4`
for ametryn, `ecxwb1` for atrazine, `ecx4param` for diuron and irgarol, `ecxll3`
for hexazinone and simazine, and `ecxwb2p3` for tebuthiuron. That is the
reason to build the model this way rather than to fit one equation to all of
them. It is also what the herbicide set looks like generally: the weight each
chosen equation holds at its own level runs from 0.279 for diuron to 0.623 for
hexazinone, and is below 0.4 for five of the seven.

Every estimate from a joint refit reports per level, one row each, which is the
shape `bnec_group()` returns.


``` r
ecx(herb_joint, ecx_val = 50, xform = exp)
#>         level         Q50        Q2.5       Q97.5 bound_Q50 bound_Q2.5 bound_Q97.5
#> 1     ametryn   1.5040983   1.4216626   1.6062783                                 
#> 2    atrazine  40.0880590  35.9270004  44.5171742                                 
#> 3      diuron   2.0212941   1.9027720   2.1445013                                 
#> 4  hexazinone   7.4412827   6.8529383   8.0858175                                 
#> 5     irgarol   0.5379826   0.4939557   0.5946915                                 
#> 6    simazine 126.6209286 117.1441126 136.7584620                                 
#> 7 tebuthiuron  90.9676220  86.7387337  95.2485272
```

The contrast is then taken on the draws. `posterior = TRUE` returns the
per-level draws as a named list, and because they come from one fit they are
already aligned: draw *i* of one level and draw *i* of another were taken at the
same step of the same chain.


``` r
herb_draws <- ecx(herb_joint, ecx_val = 50, posterior = TRUE, xform = exp)
diuron_irgarol <- herb_draws[["diuron"]] - herb_draws[["irgarol"]]
c(prob_diuron_higher = mean(diuron_irgarol > 0),
  median_difference = median(diuron_irgarol),
  quantile(diuron_irgarol, c(0.025, 0.975)))
#> prob_diuron_higher  median_difference               2.5%              97.5% 
#>           1.000000           1.481583           1.353796           1.613279
```

Diuron exceeds irgarol in every draw, by 1.48 µg/L (1.35 to 1.61). Read on the
N(S)EC instead --- the quantity `compare_posterior()` was given above --- the
same pair gives:


``` r
herb_ne_draws <- nsec(herb_joint, posterior = TRUE, xform = exp)
diuron_irgarol_ne <- herb_ne_draws[["diuron"]] - herb_ne_draws[["irgarol"]]
c(prob_diuron_higher = mean(diuron_irgarol_ne > 0),
  median_difference = median(diuron_irgarol_ne),
  quantile(diuron_irgarol_ne, c(0.025, 0.975)))
#> prob_diuron_higher  median_difference               2.5%              97.5% 
#>         0.79162500         0.01951490        -0.03127141         0.06660047
```

a probability of 0.79 that diuron's is the higher, with a median difference of
0.020 µg/L (-0.031 to 0.067). `compare_posterior()` gave 0.727. The two routes
agree in direction, and neither separates this pair on the N(S)EC.

That split between the two estimates is the one the zinc case study met as well.
An ECx is a fixed drop from each level's own control and is read where the curve
is steep; the N(S)EC is a departure from a control band, and a small shift in
where that band ends puts the crossing a long way further along a curve that is
nearly flat there.

The joint refit sampled without difficulty, across a model estimating five
distinct functional forms and a separate dispersion for each of seven levels:


``` r
np <- brms::nuts_params(herb_joint$fit)
s_joint <- summary(herb_joint$fit)
pars <- rbind(s_joint$fixed, s_joint$spec_pars)
c(divergent = sum(np$Value[np$Parameter == "divergent__"]),
  post_warmup_draws = sum(np$Parameter == "divergent__"),
  max_rhat = max(pars$Rhat), min_bulk_ess = min(pars$Bulk_ESS))
#>         divergent post_warmup_draws          max_rhat      min_bulk_ess 
#>          0.000000       8000.000000          1.001624       5372.675436
```

no divergent transitions in 8000 post-warmup draws, a maximum R-hat of 1.002 and
a minimum bulk effective sample size of 5373.

One caution survives all of this. A joint refit conditions on one equation per
level, so the model uncertainty the per-level averages represent is absent from
it. Here the difference is small: irgarol's EC50 spans 0.494 to 0.595 µg/L in
the joint refit, a factor of 1.20, against 0.491 to 0.598 and a factor of 1.22
from `fits_herb`, because the equations irgarol's weight is spread over agree
closely on its EC50. Where they disagree, the joint refit's interval is narrower
than the per-level one by that disagreement. Where the chosen equation holds
most of a level's weight, that narrowing is a real gain in precision. Where it
holds 0.291, as irgarol's does, it would be uncertainty set aside rather than
resolved.

The two routes therefore answer different questions, and neither is a correction
of the other. `compare_posterior()` asks how two independently estimated
herbicides compare, each with its own model uncertainty, which is what a
reader wants when the seven were tested separately and are being ranked. The
joint refit asks how two levels of one model compare, holding the dispersion
structure and the sampling common between them, which is what a reader wants
when the question is whether these two differ. The herbicide case study reports
the model-averaged per-level estimates for the first reason; a controlled
contrast --- a treatment against its control, two sites of one experiment ---
is the second.


# Choosing a route for a factor

Three routes fit a factor, and they answer different questions. The choice is
made from the question rather than from the data, because all three will return
an answer on any dataset with enough levels.

| the question | the route | the call |
|---|---|---|
| Does the shape of the curve differ between levels? | separate fits | `bnec_group(y ~ crf(x, "all"), group_var = "site")` |
| What is the population curve, with the differences between levels treated as nuisance? | a group-level term | `y ~ crf(x, "all") + ogl(site)` |
| What is the difference between two named levels, within one posterior? | a joint refit | `bnec_joint(fits)` on a `bnec_group()` fit |

Separate fits are the only route that lets the functional form differ between
levels. Each level gets its own model set and its own weights, so one level may
be described by `nec3param` and another by `ecxll5`, and the herbicide case
study above is that case. In exchange nothing is shared: each level is
estimated from its own data alone, and a level with few observations is
estimated imprecisely.

A group-level term shares everything except the deviations it names. It is the
route for a grouping that is a nuisance rather than a subject --- plates,
chambers, tanks --- where the levels are exchangeable and the question is about
the population curve rather than about any level. `ogl()` displaces the whole
curve, `pgl()` gives every parameter its own deviation, and `(par | group)`
names one parameter. The zinc case study above chooses between them by fitting
all three and reading the group-level standard deviations, which is the general
method: the term is a claim about which differences exist, and the standard
deviations say whether the data support it.

A joint refit estimates every level's curve parameters in one posterior, with
no pooling between them. It is reached from a `bnec_group()` fit rather than
from a formula, so the equation is chosen against the per-level model weights
before it is refitted. Two things follow that neither other route gives. A
contrast between levels is a difference within one posterior rather than
between two independent ones, so it can condition on what the levels share.
And the dispersion can be estimated across levels rather than per level, which
is the right model where the measurement error is a property of the assay and
not of the level. See `?bnec_joint`.

The comparison in *Within-concentration grouping* and *Across-concentration
grouping* above is between the first two routes on one dataset, and its result
does not transfer: `ogl(conc_group)` widened the intervals and `ogl(plate)`
narrowed them, on the same response, because a grouping whose levels sit at one
concentration and a grouping whose levels span the series have different work to
do. What transfers is the method, which is to fit the alternatives and read the
standard deviations rather than to argue from the design.


# Provenance

Every fit shown was made when this vignette was precompiled, so the estimates
are those of the package version it ships with. The session that produced them
is recorded below.


``` r
packageVersion("bayesnec")
#> [1] '2.1.3.41'
packageVersion("brms")
#> [1] '2.23.0'
R.version.string
#> [1] "R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24)"
```

The fits use `model = "all"`, which `bnec()` filters to the equations valid for
the family and predictor. Three groups of calls do not. The herbicide call uses
`decline`, to match Figure 11 of @fisher2024. The parameter-count contrast on
`coral_colour` names two equations on each side, because the contrast is the
point. The named-parameter fits on `zn15` name `nec3param` and `nec4param`. No
call names `iter`, `warmup` or `control`, so `bnec()`'s defaults apply: 4 chains
at 10000 iterations with 8000 warmup, under `seed = 228`. `bnec()` also raises
`adapt_delta` from Stan's 0.8 to 0.99 of its own accord for an equation whose
mean a group-level term could still place outside the family's support. Here
that is the hormesis equations `nechorme`, `nechorme4`, `nechormepwr01` and
`ecxhormebc4` in the fits with a group-level term; the other equations sampled
at 0.8. Under the package's previous default priors, `ecxll5` returned 880
divergent transitions of 16000 on the single-plate fit at 0.8. It now returns
none on that fit at the same 0.8, and holds 0.12 of the weight.

@luter2025 sampled the published `lum31` analysis longer again, at 20000
iterations with 19000 warmup and `adapt_delta = 0.99` named explicitly.

`ecxhormebc5` is excluded before fitting wherever the predictor reaches a
negative value and the response family requires a positive mean on an identity
link. Its hormesis term `exp(slope) * x` is negative wherever the predictor is,
and a starting value drawn from the prior then puts the mean below zero, which
neither a Gamma nor a `Beta` on an identity link can represent. That covers
every fit in this vignette on a logged predictor: the `lum31` concentrations
are in mg/L and negative on the log scale for 60 per cent of the zinc readings
at 15 minutes and 74 per cent of the copper ones,
and `log(diuron_adj)` is negative below 1 µg/L. `necsigm` and `ecxsigm` are
excluded on the same predictor for a different reason, that a fractional power
of a negative number is undefined. See #344.

`lum31` was built from the AIMS data repository deposit accompanying
@luter2025 by `data-raw/lum31.R`. `coral_colour` and `coral_pam` were built from
the records behind @flores2021 by `data-raw/coral_diuron.R`. Neither set of
source records is distributed with the package: the scripts are, and the
manual pages state what was derived and how.
